transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-14 14:00 PST | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Olivia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Bell (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Ortiz (Head of ML, Sytox), Pavel Ivanov (Platform Eng), Marta Sousa (CTO)

[00:00] Olivia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Olivia from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, with Marcus who's our solutions engineer. How're you all doing?
[00:06] Marta: Good thanks, hi. We kicked off a quick agenda in the invite: model choices, context length, multi-ling support and tool calling.
[00:12] Lena: Yes, we have quite a few questions. We're building a clinical triage assistant for telehealth intake, so prompts can be very long — patient history, prior notes, attachments.
[00:18] Marcus: Got it. Can you share a rough distribution of sequence lengths? avg vs 95th?
[00:22] Pavel: Average is around 3k tokens but 95th is close to 55k today because clinicians paste long histories. We are considering a 64k window as a minimum, maybe 128k for future.
[00:32] Olivia: Ok that maps to a few different product decisions — hosted can support large context via our curated 64k and 128k variants for certain models, dedicated gives you reserved capacity and better predictability, and private (VPC/on-prem) if you need network isolation and control over keys.
[00:44] Marta: For us, security is non-negotiable. SOC 2 is a must. We also need KMS integration (HSM preferred) and SSO/SAML.
[00:51] Marcus: We support SOC 2, SAML SSO, and KMS integrations. For Private we can support customer-managed keys via KMS or integrated HSM depending on deployment.
[00:58] Lena: One other big piece is tool calling — the assistant needs to make structured calls into our EMR and also kick off lab order flows. That requires function or tool calling and fine-grained RBAC.
[01:06] Marcus: Yep, our hosted API supports function-calling patterns and structured output. For dedicated or private you can run tool proxies inside VPC so calls to EMR never traverse public internet.
[01:14] Pavel: How reliable is the function-calling when we do heavy load? We're planning spikes during morning rounds.
[01:19] Marcus: On Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools and autoscale policies that handle spikes predictably; hosted has burst, but if you need strict SLOs Dedicated is safer. There's also the caching and batching layer — prefix caching can reduce cost for repeated contexts.
[01:29] Marta: Cost is also a blocker — we have to balance latency for real-time triage vs units cost. Any ways to reduce token cost without losing quality?
[01:36] Olivia: A few levers: model selection (smaller quantized models), KV/prefix caching, token trimming heuristics, and routing policies that send low-risk requests to cheaper variants. Marcus can share Optimize suggestions after a quick eval.
[01:45] Marcus: I'll add recommendations to the runbook. On models: you said open models — which families are you evaluating?
[01:50] Lena: We're looking at Mistral-7B/Chat variants, Llama 2 derivatives, and a couple of opt/bert hybrids from community. Also curious about emergent behavior in longer context.
[01:58] Marcus: For long context you want architectures that handle attention efficiently. Some community quant profiles behave poorly beyond 32k. We have verified profiles for several open models at 64k and 128k but quality varies. For medical domain we usually run small fine-tunes or instruction-tuning on curated prompts.
[02:12] Pavel: Are the verified profiles in a public doc?
[02:15] Olivia: We'll share the model performance sheet — Marcus will put the link in the notes (link: https://redwood.ai/bench/sytox-2026).
[02:22] Marta: Multilingual — Portuguese and Spanish are 30% of our volume. How do open models compare?
[02:27] Marcus: Llama variants often do OK on Spanish, less so on Portuguese. Some Mistral-family and Mosaic variants have better multilingual consistency. We recommend evaluating with your actual prompts — we'll run a bilingual benchmark.
[02:37] Lena: Also hallucination safety. When the model calls tools we need a high correctness bar and deterministic extraction of entities for orders.
[02:44] Marcus: Tool calling plus a deterministic post-processing layer is the usual pattern. We can also enforce guardrails via model output schemas and use lightweight rerankers or validators. For critical actions like lab orders we recommend a confirmation step in workflow.
[02:56] Pavel: On the network side — we have strict egress policies. Private is probably preferred but it raises cost and ops overhead. Any guidance?
[03:03] Marcus: Private gives you the most control — customer-managed control plane in VPC, or an on-prem package for air-gapped. Dedicated with private networking (VPC peering and private IPs) can be a middle ground: less ops than full on-prem, but still no internet egress for inference calls.
[03:17] Marta: Sizing: What GPU profiles do you recommend for 64k context at scale?
[03:22] Marcus: For 64k you'll likely want A100-80GB equivalents with memory-optimized stacks and efficient kernel selection. For 128k we typically shard across multiple devices or use model variants compiled for long attention. We'll propose a few SKU options in the benchmarking playbook.
[03:35] Lena: Do you support quantized FP4/INT4 for these open models? We're cost-conscious.
[03:39] Marcus: Yes, our runtime supports low-bit quantization profiles, but low-bit can affect accuracy on medical extraction tasks. We usually recommend a mixed profile: quantize transformer layers but keep final layers in higher precision. That trades cost for quality.
[03:51] Olivia: Quick check — timeline and stakeholders? Marta: compliance and platform sign-off will need to be engaged this month. Implementation team is Pavel and Lena. CTO Marta will sign for exec.
[04:02] Marta: Budget window is H1 with pilot in Feb if numbers look right.
[04:06] Olivia: Great. We'll aim to get pricing and pilot plan to you by 1/18, then run a 2-week pilot where we'll run the benchmark on your sample prompts and live-ish traffic.
[04:14] Pavel: Ok, what do you need from us to kick off the benchmark?
[04:17] Marcus: Sample prompt set, redaction rules, expected qps and peak concurrency, and a small dataset for multilingual tests. Also network constraints for VPC peering. We'll provide the runbook and a Jenkins/CI job if you want.
[04:29] Lena: We have some sensitive PHI; can we redact locally before sending or run pilot inside our VPC?
[04:35] Marcus: Both possible. If you run a private pilot inside your VPC with our on-prem agent, PHI never leaves customer network. Alternatively you can locally redact or tokenise data before sending to hosted endpoints.
[04:45] Marta: Are audit logs available for all flows? We need retention for 7 years for certain records.
[04:50] Marcus: Audit logs are available with Dedicated and Private, and with Hosted we offer audit logs for enterprise tiers with configurable retention. We'll include logging SLAs in the security docs.
[04:59] Olivia: Competitors question — you've mentioned Anthropic and OpenAI. Any specific concerns?
[05:03] Marta: Mainly lock-in and cost predictability, and ability to run in our cloud region. Also model transparency for audits.
[05:10] Marcus: Those are common concerns. With Redwood you can pin model versions, roll back, and we provide signed SBOMs and model provenance metadata for audits.
[05:18] (crosstalk) Pavel: sorry quick question on latency — for triage we need sub-500ms token latency end-to-end ideally.
[05:24] Marcus: Sub-500ms per token is aggressive for long context but achievable if you route short queries to smaller models and reserve capacity for real-time paths. Streaming responses and local caching reduce perceived latency.
[05:34] Lena: Could you walk through an example run — patient note posted, model calls tool X, confirmation, lab order — and where data sits?
[05:40] Marcus: Sure. Example: 1) request hits Redwood API -> routing decides model and runtime. 2) model produces tool call payload (structured) -> Redwood proxies the call to your EMR via private integration or customer proxy. 3) a lightweight validator checks payload against schema -> confirmation prompt sent back to clinician. Data residency depends on deployment: hosted by Redwood (encrypted at rest, KMS), dedicated VPC (your network boundaries), private on-prem (stay local).
[06:02] Marta: That sounds good. For our compliance team we need architecture diagrams and the runbook.
[06:07] Olivia: We'll attach architecture diagrams and Marcus will include the runbook + benchmark template link.
[06:12] (pause)
[06:20] Marcus: I'll also note caveats for long-context with certain open model variants — some community checkpoints drop accuracy around 64k. We'll propose a shortlist: 1) Mistral-long-64k verified, 2) Llama-deriv-128k (cust-compiled), 3) Mosaic-multi-64k for multilingual.
[06:36] Lena: Any examples of customers doing similar clinical workflows?
[06:39] Olivia: We have a few anonymized case studies — we'll share a redacted version focusing on triage use-cases and safety patterns.
[06:47] Pavel: For the pilot, can we run a small on-prem cluster for the heavy-context scenarios?
[06:52] Marcus: Yes, we support an on-prem package. It requires some initial setup but gives you full control and no egress. We'll provide a checklist.
[06:59] Marta: Ok last question: function-calling determinism — does Redwood provide deterministic output enforcement or we need to implement validators?
[07:05] Marcus: We provide structured output schema enforcement and optional lightweight reranking or constrained decoding layers. For mission-critical actions we recommend validators as an additional safety net.
[07:16] Olivia: Great — wrap up quick recap and next steps?
[07:19] Marcus: Recap: 1) Need benchmark template + runbook (Marcus) 2) Pricing + pilot SKUs (Olivia) 3) Sytox to provide sample prompts, redaction rules, and QPS profile (Lena/Pavel) 4) Schedule pilot kickoff week of 1/26.
[07:32] Marta: Fine. We'll aim to get prompts by 1/20.
[07:36] Olivia: Perfect. I'll follow up with a calendar invite for the kickoff and attach the links. The benchmark link again: https://redwood.ai/bench/sytox-2026 (will include scoring sheets).
[07:45] Lena: Thanks. One small note — please include an example of a tool-call schema for our EMR.
[07:49] Marcus: Will do, I'll add an example payload and validation snippet.
[07:53] Pavel: Thanks all.
[07:55] Olivia: Thanks everyone, talk soon.

(End of recording)

Notes: Transcription contains occasional mis-hearings; timestamps approximate. Shared artifacts: deck (link: https://redwood.ai/decks/sytox-jan14), benchmark sheet (https://redwood.ai/bench/sytox-2026).

Security checklist items to send: SOC 2 report, KMS integration guide, on-prem deployment checklist, audit log retention options.
